Geophys. J. R. asp. SOC.( 1980) 60,355-375
The palaeomagnetism of Jersey volcanics and dykes,
and the Lower Palaeozoic apparent polar wander
path for Europe
B. A. Duff *
Department of Earth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT
Received 1979 May 4
Summary. Stable natural remanent magnetization (NRM) in the Jersey
Volcanics and in a single rhyolite dyke was probably acquired during the
Cambrian before folding of the volcanics in the Cadomian Orogeny. After dip
correction, the volcanics yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 323" E, 52" N (dp =
33", dm=35"). In Jersey dolerite dykes three groups of stable NRM direc-
tions are recognized, with palaeomagnetic poles at 248' E, 26" N (dp = lo",
dm = 20°), 339" E, 1" S (dp = 9", dm = 12"), and 336" E, 31" S (dp = 5",
dm = 9"). Comparison with the European apparent polar wander path implies
that stable NRM in these groups was acquired respectively during Late
Precambrian or early Cambrian, Siluro-Devonian and middle Carboniferous
time. The stable NRM of the Jersey lamprophyre dykes yields a palaeomag-
netic pole at 322" E, 16" N (dp = 31°, dm = 38") and is probably of Silurian
or Devonian age.
These palaeomagnetic poles and other new data determined by the author
for the Armorican Massif can be fitted to a common apparent polar wander
path for Europe, and this implies that the basement of Lower Palaeozoic
Europe extended from the Baltic Shield at least as far south as the Armorican
Massif. The Hercynian Orogeny in these parts of Europe was therefore
probably intracratonic. This polar wander path implies that in early Cambrian
time the pole did not move significantly relative to Europe, but that this was
followed by a large middle to late Cambrian polar shift which corresponded
to rapid drift of Europe across the South Pole.
1 The Jersey Volcanics
1.1 INTRODUCTION
Acid and intermediate volcanics (Mourant 1933) crop out mainly in north-east Jersey, and
were sampled as part of a palaeomagnetic survey of the island to improve the Lower Palaeo-
zoic palaeomagnetic record of western Europe. The basal volcanic unit, the Jersey Andesite

Formation, overlies Upper Brioverian metasediments (Mourant 1933) and is overlain,
probably unconformably, by rhyolites, tuffs and ignimbrites.
The age of the Jersey Andesite Formation has been estimated at 533 f 16Myr (middle
Cambrian) by Rb-Sr whole rock dating (hRb = 1.39 X lo-" yr; Duff 1978a). The acid
volcanics, too, are probably not much younger than middle Cambrian because they are over-
lain unconfomably by the Rozel Conglomerate which is considered to be Cambrian. or
Ordovician (e.g. Renouf 1974).
Palaeomagnetic collections of the acid volcanics were made at several rhyolite, tuff and
ignimbrite sites along the wellexposed section on the east coast north of Gorey, and at four
sites on or near the north coast (Fig. 1). A rhyolite dyke (site 59) was sampled east of
Mont Orgueil Castle. The Jersey Andesite Formation was sampled on the eastern shore of
St Aubin's Bay (Fig. 1).
1.2 NRM OF THE JERSEY VOLCANICS
Intensities of total NRM for the 13 rhyolite, tuff and ignimbrite sites ranged from about
lod4 to 6 X Am-'. The rhyolite dyke (site J9) and the andesites possessed much larger
intensities of up to 1.5 X lo-' and 5 X lo-' Am-' respectively. Site mean directions of total
NRM before dip correction are either very steep or variably inclined south-westerly down-
ward directions (Fig. 2(a)); correction for structural dip results in a slightly larger scatter of
directions (Fig. 2(b)).
With two exceptions (sites SC1 and SC2) all acid volcanic sites and the andesite site are
stable against alternating field (a.f.) demagnetization. Typically, a quarter of the original
NRM remains after demagnetization in peak fields from about 100 to 160mT, and direc-
tions of NRM are consistent over this range of applied fields (e.g. dip-corrected directions

indicate that haematite is the main remanence carrier.
The rhyolite dyke and andesites are less resistant to a.f. demagnetization (Fig. 3(d)) than
the acid volcanics, and this is consistent with indications that magnetite carries most of the
NRM in the dyke and andesites. Three-quarters of the original dyke NRM is demagnetized
in peak fields of 30mT. Most acid volcanic sites and the rhyolite dyke yield steep endpoints
(dip corrected, Fig. 3(b)-(d)).
Some specimens from sites J19, 535, AC and LC gave a.f. demagnetization trends sugges-
tive of multi-component NRM (e.g. Fig. 3(e)). The in situ NRM directions of separate
specimens in these sites after demagnetization in progressively higher fields converge toward
a south-westerly direction with an intermediate, downward inclination which corresponds
to a hard component acquired after folding of the volcanics. This direction is close to the
Devonian direction of south-west Europe.

stable single component NRM (e.g. Fig. 3(f) and (8)) indicates that the NRM is distributed

The magnetite-bearing rhyolite dyke from Mont Orgueil has a distributed blocking tempera-
ture spectrum with the bulk of single component NRM in the range 0-250°C (Fig. 3(h)),
and consistent NRM directions up to 450°C similar to the dip-corrected directions isolated
in most acid volcanic sites by both a.f. and thermal demagnetization.
1.3 ANALYSIS OF NRM DIRECTIONS
Thermal and a.f. demagnetization show that a minority of sites possess two components of
NRM, one acquired before and one after folding. At the majority of sites, where NRM is
single-component it is therefore important to determine if it was acquired before or after
folding.
In this respect, the direction of stable NRM in the rhyolite dyke is important for the
interpretation of the NkM directions of the volcanics. This dyke is of very similar composi-
tion to the acid volcanic flows which were sampled, and may have been a contemporaneous
feeder for those flows (Mourant 1933). Because the dyke has not been folded or tilted since
emplacement, its NRM direction is unambiguous. In contrast with most in situ site mean
results, the dip-corrected mean directions of several sites (Fig. 2) are close to the steep
direction characteristic of the dyke. This implies that at least for many sites, NRM was
acquired before folding as a single component with steep inclination.
Sites with low stability against a.f. demagnetization and sites with many specimens
containing variable multi-component NRM were excluded from the overall analysis. The dip-
corrected NRM directions from the remaining 10 sites (Fig. 2(d)) are distributed about a
mean D = 292", Z = 78" with precision K = 7.7. A two-tier analysis (Watson & Irving 1957) of
the dip-corrected NRM directions of the 10 sites implies a significant between-site scatter at
the 99 per cent probability level; between-site scatter (0 = 9.4) is the main source of overall
disperson.
It is likely that a large part of the between-site scatter of NRM directions in acid volcanics
results from the extremely viscous nature of acid flows, as a result of penecontemporaneous

Comparison of the in situ and dip-corrected between-site precisions for the 10 site mean
directions of NRM by Cox's (1969) method indicates that the estimates of the 95 per cent
probability level confidence intervals flu, fll about the true precision for the in situ directions

although the difference between in situ and dip-corrected precisions favours the view that

site mean directions in the volcanics with the direction of stable NRM in the rhyolite dyke.
The best estimate of NRM direction in the Jersey Volcanics is therefore the dip-corrected
mean of site mean directions 6=292", 1=78" (a9,= 19"), which yields a palaeomagnetic
pole at 323" E, 52"N (dp =33", dm =35"; Table 1). The large oval of confidence about the
mean pole is a consequence of dipole field properties at high latitude (see, for example,
Irving 1964, Figure 4.7).
1.4 THE ORIGIN AND AGE OF NRM IN THE JERSEY VOLCANICS
The very high stabilities of NRM against a.f. demagnetization and thermomagnetic results
suggest that the dominant magnetic phase and carrier of NRM in the rhyolites, tuffs and
ignimbrites is haematite. In these rocks small regions of relict magnetite occur within octa-
hedral crystals of haematite, which is arranged in a mesh texture parallel to the vestigial
octahedral cleavage. These features suggest that original magnetite has been pseudomorphed
by haematite during martitization. In some ignimbrite sites haematite is mainly contained
within phenocrysts of amphibole or biotite,
Oxidation of biotite to haematite is common in volcanic rocks (Eugster & Wones 1962);
it proceeds first - perhaps before extrusion - to magnetite and alkali feldspar, and after
extrusion magnetite is oxidized, partially or completely, to haematite. Much of the haema-
tite in the Jersey Volcanics was probably derived from magnetite during the initial cooling

of the lava pile. The magnetite may in turn have been derived from primal, ferromagnesian
phenocrysts, or have crystallized independently.
The main Fe-Ti oxide in the rhyolite dyke is magnetite, which is present as discrete
octahedral crystals. The presence of magnetite in the dyke in contrast to the haematite of
the extrusives presumably reflects the higher oxygen fugacities of the extrusives on surface
.
cooling
According to the thermal demagnetization results, temperatures of about 2OO0C (PulIaiah
ef al 1975) over sustained periods (> 1 Myr) would have been necessary for the NRM associ-
ated with the initial formation of haematite to have been subsequently reset. However, the
pre-tectonic folding age of the NRM of the volcanics suggests that the burial necessary for
such remagnetization has not occurred. The age of crystallization estimated for the Jersey
Andesite Formation provides a maximum age for the overlying acid volcanics. Folding of
the Jersey Volcanics occurred during the Cadomian Orogeny before deposition of the Rozel
Conglomerate in late Cambrian or early Ordovician times. The bulk of stable NRM was
therefore probably acquired during the interval 533 Myr (middle Cambrian) to early
Ordovician.
2 Jersey dolerite and lamprophyre dykes
2.1 INTRODUCTION
Palaeomagnetic collections were made of 29 dolerite dykes intrusive into the south-east
granite and diorite, the south-west granite and the Brioverian metasediments, and eight
lamprophyre dykes intrusive into the three granites, the southeast diorite and the Rozel
Conglomerate of Jersey (Fig. 1). The ages of the dolerite dykes have not been determined,
although both dolerites and lamprophyres must by younger than the granites and diorites
(Late Precambrian to Ordovician). A lamprophyre which intrudes the Rozel Conglomerate
*
has yielded a K-Ar hornblende age of 427 13M yr (Adams 1967).
2.2 NRM OF THE JERSEY DOLERITES AND LAMPROPHYRES
Dolerite and lamprophyre dyke mean directions of total NRM(Fig. 4) are scattered,although
most are steep and downward pointing. Intensities of NRM in the dolerites and lampro-
phyres range from to 10 Am'
On a.f. demagnetization in peak fields up to lOOmT, 21 of the 29 dolerite dykes yielded
stable endpoints (Fig. 5). Magnetic cleaning of 18 of the 21 stable dykes yielded three
distinct palaeomagnetic groupings of dyke mean directions (Fig. 4(b)). These are distinguished
entirely on palaeomagnetic grounds; there are no cross-cutting relationships between the
dykes in the three groups which could support the distinction as reflecting differences in
relative age of the dyke groups, although group C dykes all belong to a swarm of wide,
north-east-trending dykes. Dykes of group A have shallow, downward south-south-west
stable NRM directions; group B dykes are magnetized steeply downwards to the south-west
(although one dyke from St. Brelade has an NRM direction reversed with respect to this
group); and group C dykes have shallow downward or upward north-west directions (Fig. 4).
Three dykes (JlO, 533 and 542) gave directions of stable NRM oblique to these groups
(Fig. 5(e) and (f)).
Group A dykes intrude an older phase of the south-west granite and the south-east granite
near Dicq. They are mainly east or east-north-east-trending dykes of variable thickness
(40cm to 5m). The stable NRM of group A dykes generally resides in coercivities of
remanence from 0 to 60mT (Fig. 5(a)).

23 THERMOMAGNETIC AND OPTICAL ANALYSIS
2-3.1 Jersey dolerites
Two groups of Curie points associated with two distinct types of thermomagnetic curve
(M,(T) curve) characterize the Jersey dolerites. Dykes with Curie points of 500-600°C
characteristic of titanium poor or pure magnetite (Fig. 7(b) and (c)) have N6el's (1948) Q
type or nearly straight heating curves. In contrast, high Curie points up to 770°C are associ-
ated with concave heating curves, and possibly reflect the presence of maghaemite (Fig. 7(a)
and (d)). These characterize most group A dykes and also dykes JlO,J33 and J15.
Different dykes within the three palaeomagnetic groups, and the dykes with unstable
NRM have M,(T) curves that are either Q type, straight or concave; there is no consistency
ofM,(T) curve or Curie points within groups. This implies that the NRM groupings were not
controlled by systematic differences in magnetic mineralogy.

Figure 7. Thermomagnetic curves for Jersey dolerites.
Reflected light observations indicate that light brown or grey magnetite is the most
common magnetic phase in the Jersey dolerites. It is present as discrete homogeneous
crystals with few or no observable ilmenite or haematite lamellae, and therefore belongs to
the lowest oxidation classes 1 and 2 (Wilson & Haggerty 1966). The steel grey colour of the
magnetites in some dykes, especially those in group C, and the relatively high Curie points
suggest that the magGCtites contain little titanium. The paradox of high Curie points of
magnetites in basic rocks (which are expected to be high in titanium and hence have relatively
low Curie points) has been discussed by Ade-Hall (1964), Ade-Hall, Wilson & Smith (1965)
and Creer, Hedley & O’Reilly (1975) with reference to basic extrusives. Following these
authors, the high Curie points of the Jersey dolerites are ascribed to submicroscopic unmix-
ing of titanium poor magnetite. Of the dykes with Curie points characteristic of maghaemite,
only 531 and 533 show alteration of magnetite to maghaemite. Maghaemite may be present
as submicroscopic grains in the other dykes.
Haematite is present in minor amounts associated with the magnetites as marginal grains
and patchy inclusions. In a few of the palaeomagnetically unstable dykes, ilmenite is the
main oxide phase and is typically present as large homogeneous phenocrysts, some of which
have hollow cores.
2.3.2 Jersey lamprophyres
Most lamprophyre dykes have Q type M,(T) curves with Curie points characteristic of
titanium poor or pure magnetite. The mean Curie point estimated from the Q type heating

Ti,,, 04.D ykes 513 and 522 gave concaveq(2') curves with high Curie points appropriate
to titanohaematite (640°C) and possibly maghaemite (730°C) respectively.
Reflected light microscopy also suggests that the dominant magnetic phase is titanium-
poor magnetite. Fine haematite lamellae comprise a few per cent of the magnetites of some
dykes but typically haematite is absent, and the magnetites are unoxidized and homogeneous
(oxidation class 1 of Wilson & Haggerty 1966), unless submicroscopic unmixing has occurred.
No magnetic phases were observed in two of the palaeomagnetically stable lamprophyres
despite indications of the presence of magnetite from thermomagnetic analysis. This suggests
that the stable NRM may be carried by submicroscopic magnetite.
2.4 MEAN DIRECTIONS OF NRM AND PALAEOMAGNETICP OLE POSITIONS
Mean directions of stable NRM for the three dolerite groups and the lamprophyre dykes
(except 518) are shown in Fig. 4(b), and summarized in Table 1. A mean direction of NRM
is given for group C dykes, although the large scatter of directions between dykes in this
swarm (K = 10; u95= 20') is noted. The stable NRM in group C dykes is believed to be Late
Precambrian to early Cambrian in age (Section 3.2), and the scatter in this group may reflect
real variations in the Late Precambrian geomagnetic field, as rocks with NRM of similar age in
Denmark, the Nexd Sandstone, also record a large between-site scatter (Prasad & Sharma
1978).
The three stable dolerite dykes with large within-dyke scatter of NRM directions, oblique
to directions in the three groups, were excluded from the group analysis. The stable lampro-
phyre dyke, 518, has a mean direction D = 41", I= -19', which is significantly different at
the 95 per cent probability level from the other stable dyke groups; it was also excluded
from the overall analysis.
3 Palaeozoic apparent polar wander and its geological implications
3.1 THE APPARENT POLAR WANDER PATH FOR EUROPE
3.1.1 Introduction
The European Lower Palaeozoic apparent polar wander (apw) path is poorly known and
published paths have been based Oil results mainly from Britain and Norway. The single
British pole position from rocks of Cambrian age -the Lower Cambrian Caerfai Series
(Briden, Irons &Johnson 1970) differs from that from the Lower Cambrian Fen Carbona-
-
tite complex (Poorter 1972) of Norway. A controversial discrepancy between Norwegian
and British Siluro-Devonian results has been explained by complex remagnetization of the
British rocks (e.g. Storetvedt & Halvorsen 1968), by Lower Palaeozoic relative movements
between the Baltic Shield and Britain (Briden, Morris & Piper 1973), and by reinterpretation
of the magnetization ages for the Norwegian rocks (McElhinny & Briden 1971).
It is doubtful whether the Caerfai Series pole reflects a Cambrian magnetization. The
location of the series close to the Hercynian front in Wales, and the position of its pole close
to well-established Carboniferous poles for Europe suggest that the Caerfai Series was
remagnetized during the Hercynian Orogeny.
The oldest palaeomagnetic pole positions on the British path of Briden et al. (1973) are
therefore of Ordovician age. New data from Jersey (including the results from the Jersey
volcanics and dykes described in this paper), the Armorican massif (Duff 1979a), Leicester-
shire (Duff 1979b), and a minor study in North Wales (Duff 1978b) are summarized in

The new results from the Armorican Massif help define the Cambrian segment of the apw
path. Means of polar groupings confirm the Ordovician to Carboniferous segments of the
published apw path for Britain and lie on the same path as the Norwegian pole positions.
3.1.2 Precambrian to Cambrian
A Precambrian south apw path for Europe is tentatively suggested in Fig. 8(a) based on the
Precambrian palaeomagnetic data from the Baltic Shield and Britain, including the Channel
Islands. The pole moves from the southern hemisphere first north-east towards the equator
then northwards across the equator to a position defined by poles from the 600Myr Mona
Complex (Piper 1976), the Longmynd dykes (Lomax & Briden 1977), the in situ or dip-
corrected St. Peter Port Gabbro (E. Hailwood, private communication) of Late Precambrian
to early Cambrian age, the Jersey group C dolerite dykes, and the Nexd Sandstone (Prasad
& Sharma 1978). This is followed by a large apparent polar shift to the early Cambrian
group.
The most novel feature of the apw path is that an early Cambrian quasi-static interval is
followed by a large polar shift. The quasi-static interval is defined by the poles from the
Fen complex of Norway (Poorter 1972), Leicestershire diorites, and a preliminary result
from red shales in the Lower Cambrian of North Wales (Duff 1978b). This last result was
based on five samples collected by M. P. Coward from Bangor (lat. 53.3" N; long. 356" E)
which gave the following preliminary results: D = 206"; I = -40"; N = 5; R = 4.73; K = 15;
ag, = 21". The corresponding VGP is at 132' E 54" N. The pole then appears to have moved
rapidly via high latitudes (defined by the Jersey granites, the Uriconian and Malvernian, and
possibly the Longmynd sediments) through intermediate latitudes (defined by the Jersey
Volcanics, the in situ Mona Complex and the Erquy Spilite Series) and thence towards low
latitudes and on the Ordovician segment of the apw path (Fig. 8(b)). Rb-Sr whole rock
results from the Jersey Andesite Formation (Duff 1978a) suggest that this shift is, at least
partly, middle Cambrian in age. Owing to the lack of palaeomagnetic data for the period
middle Cambrian to Ordovician, the detailed nature of the apw path between the Erquy

3.1.3 Ordovician to Devonian
The Ordovician and Siluro-Devonian poles define two separate low-latitude groupings
(Table 3) as in the published British apw path (e.g. Briden et al. 1973). The pole remained
stationary with respect to Europe during the Ordovician. Most results from Ireland have not
been used in the determination of the mean Ordovician pole (Table 3) owing to evidence of
tectonic rotations within Ireland (Briden et al. 1973). Movement of the pole from the
Ordovician to the Siluro-Devonian positions could correspond to a rotation of about 30"
about a local axis (Morris 1976). Poles from the Jersey group B dolerites and lamprophyres,
and the VGP corresponding to component C in the Armorican redbeds (Duff 1979a) are all
positioned close to the mean Siluro-Devonian pole.
3.1.4 Late Devonian to late Carboniferous
Movement of the pole from its Siluro-Devonian to middle Carboniferous positions during
the late Devonian or early Carboniferous may be recorded in lavas and sediments from
Britain, Norway and the Armorican Massif. The simplest prima facie explanation of the
discrepancy between poles from British and Norwegian Siluro-Devonian rocks is that the
Norwegian (Old Red Sandstone) redbeds were remagnetized during the early Carboniferous.
This accords with the position of the Norwegian poles close to those from British early
Carboniferous rocks (see also McElhinny 1973). However, the discrepancy may alternatively
be reconciled by Devonian relative movements between the Baltic Shield and Britain (Briden
et al. 1973). Analysis of the multi-component NRM of the Armorican redbeds (Duff 1979a)
suggests that they too were remagnetized during the late Devonian or early Carboniferous.
Two distinct polar groupings defined by (i) middle to late Carboniferous and (ii) late
Carboniferous (Stephanian) to early Permian rocks, imply a polar shift during the early part
of the late Carboniferous (Fig. 8(b)). The sources of both these groups of data are spread
geographically throughout Europe. This shift,like that in the Ordovician to Siluro-Devonian
positions, corresponds to a declination change and hence could have originated by rotation
of the Palaeozoic European platform about a Euler pole close to, or on it. The declination
change shows up well in the redbeds of Normandy and Brittany (Duff 1979a) and in the
Bohemian Massif (Bir$enniajer, Krs & Nairn 1968), owing to the near-horizontal Carbon-
iferous field direction in Europe. Poles from the Jersey goup A dolerites and the TrCgastel-
Ploumanac'h complex (Duff 1979a) are positioned with the middle to late Carboniferous
group (Fig. 8(b)).
3.2 PALAEOMAGNETIC DATING
The apw path permits the ages of certain rock units hitherto of uncertain or unknown age to
be estimated. Jersey group C dolerite and Longmynd dyke pole positions are close to those
for the in situ or dip-corrected St. Peter Port Gabbro of Guernsey, which is 660 to 570Myr
old (Adams 1976), and the 600Myr Mona Complex (Piper 1976). This implies a Late
Precambrian to early Cambrian age for the Jersey group C dykes and Longmynd dykes.
Palaeomagnetic poles from the Jersey granites fall on the early to middle Cambrian (pre
533Myr) segment of the apw path, which implies that the Rb-Sr ages of the north-west
(490 f 15 Myr) and south-east (520 f 4 Myr) granitesmay underestimate the age of intrusion.
intrusion of the south-east granite by the group C dolerites with their probable Late
Precambrian to early Cambrian . magnetization, implies that the south-east granite was

The position of poles determined from post-folding remagnetizations in the Uriconian

pole’ from the Longmynd sediments (LS) may indicate a slightly younger age of remagnetiza-

Comparison of palaeomagnetic poles for group B dolerites and lamprophyre dykes with

after intrusion, group A dykes are of middle to late Carboniferous age, and were intruded
during the Hercynian Orogeny.

groupings are shown in Table 4. There have been few recent Carboniferous palaeomagnetic
studies, and the mean pole (N= 13) of McElhinny (1973) has been used for this period.
Means of natural polar groupings were determined for the Lower Palaeozoic of the Russian
and Siberian Platforms (Table 5) using the results listed by McElhinny & Cowley (1977).
The reliable poles for the Lower Palaeozoic of Australia and Africa were taken from Hail-

3.4 PALAEOLATITUDES OF EUROPE DURING THE LOWER PALAEOZOIC
The mean poles which define the apw path for Europe (Table 3) have been used to determine
the palaeolatitudes of Europe during the Lower Palaeozoic (Fig. 10). There is strong faunal
province, palaeoclimatic and stratigraphic evidence that north-west Africa, at least as far
south as the Anti-Atlas belt, was contiguous with Europe (Section 3.4.1). As its detailed
palaeoposition south of Europe is not known, north-west Africa is shown in its present-day
position relative to Europe (Fig. 10).
During the early Cambrian (Fig. lO(a)) Europe lay in low or temperate latitudes with
north-west Africa close to the equator, This is consistent with early Cambrian warm water
indicators in north-west Africa (carbonate deposits and abundant archaeocyathea; Jell 1974),
and supports the contiguity of north-west Africa with Europe'Yather than Gondwanaland,
for which near polar latitudes are predicted for northern Africa (Fig. 9; McElhinny, Giddings
& Embleton 1974). By the early to middle Cambrian Europe had drifted much closer to the
South Pole; the Baltic Shield lay in latitudes 65-80's (Fig. 10(b)). The palaeolatitudes

could accord with the evidence of glaciation in the Dalradian tillites, which are probably
partly Cambrian in age (Bennison &Wright 1969).
During the middle to late Cambrian, Europe moved around and away from the South
Pole toward low latitudes. By the Ordovician (Fig. 10(d)) the Baltic Shield and Britain were
within about 30" of the equator and north-west Africa was positioned in intermediate
latitudes. Europe rotated anticlockwise between the Ordovician (solid grid Fig. 10(d)) and
Siluro-Devonian (dashed grid), and during the early Carboniferous drifted from its Ordo-
vician to Devonian latitudes further toward the equator (Fig. lO(e)). By middle to late
Carboniferous, Britain and adjacent Europe lay on the equator. During early Late Carbon-
iferous times (Westphalian to Stephanian) the bulk of Europe rotated clockwise. This
rotation is shown in Fig. lO(f) as the corresponding change in direction of the palaeo-
meridian from middle-late Carboniferous (solid grid) to late Carboniferous (dashed grid).
3.5 THE HERCYNIAN OROGENY
3.5.1 In tegn' ty of Europe
The European Lower Palaeozoic apw path provides a common path for regions from the
Baltic Shield to at least as far south as the Armorican Massif. This suggests that the basement
of Europe extended from the Baltic Shield as far south as the Armorican Massif at least as
far back as the early Cambrian, although there may have been minor relative movements
between the Baltic Shield and Europe during Siluro-Devonian times (Briden et al. 1973).
Rapid drift during the middle and possibly late Cambrian is implied for this integral Euro-
pean block by the disparate apw paths of Europe, Russia and North America and the Lower
Palaeozoic palaeolatitudes. This was preceded by a period during the early Cambrian when
the pole remained essentially stationary relative to Europe (quasi-static interval).
A single Lower Palaeozoic Europe as extensive as present day Europe is consistent with
faunal province and stratigraphic evidence. Recent faunal province studies (Boucot, Johnson
& Talent 1969; Hallam 1973; Jell 1974) strongly suggest that Europe from the Baltic Shield
at least as far south as the Atlas belt of north-west Africa was an integral block, and this is
consistent with the continuity of the Ordovician Grb Armorican orthoquartzite facies from
Devon and Cornwall through the Armorican massif and Spain to Morocco (Renouf 1974;
Ager 1975). Detailed stratigraphic and faunal studies in the Armorican Massif and southern
England indicate that these regions were contiguous during the Lower Palaeozoic (Renouf
1974).
Although the Cambrian palaeomagnetic poles of north-west Africa (Helsley 1965; Ileana
1971; Daly & Pozzi 1977; poles shown as small diamonds in Fig. 9) may be interpreted as
falling close to the poorly defined Cambro-Ordovician segment of the African apw path, it
would be equally possible to reconcile them with the European path if their directions of
NRM have been tectonically rotated from their original declinations during the Hercynian
and Alpine deformations of north-west Africa (e.g. Sougy 1962). Early to middle Cambrian
palaeolatitudes for Europe and north-west Africa are mutually compatible.
The palaeomagnetic and geological indications of an integral European-north-west Africa
block conflict with most plate tectonic models of the Hercynian Orogeny (e.g. Burrett 1972;
Dewey & Burke 1973; Johnson 1973; Laurent 1972; McKerrow & Ziegler 1972) which
relate the acme of orogeny during the Westphalian to collision of north and south Europe,
during final closure of a mid-European sea (Whittington & Hughes 1972). These models
interpret Lower Palaeozoic deep water sediments and pillow lavas in southern England, the
Downloaded

Ardennes and the Armorican Massif as continental margin suites, contrary to the intra-
continental interpretations of detailed studies (e.g. Floyd 1972; Renouf 1974).
3.5.2 Intracratonic orogeny
The palaeomagnetic and geological evidence of an integral Lower Palaeozoic Europe-north-
west Africa block and the location of the Hercynides in Europe, are most consistent with an
intra-continental setting for the Hercynian Orogeny, although the late Carboniferous
climactic phase may have been associated with the fusion of Europe, North America and
Gondwanaland at remote continental margins. This is contrary to interpretations which
regard the Hercynian Orogeny as a continental margin type; faunal province studies suggest
that any plate margin which separated Europe and Gondwanaland should be sought south
of the Anti-Atlas belt. The relative positions of Europe-north-west Africa and the remainder
of Africa during the early Carboniferous (Fig. 9, Briden, Drewry & Smith 1974) imply that
if there was any closure between the two regions during the middle to late Carboniferous, it
was oblique (transform) rather than direct convergence.
An intracratonic interpretation of Lower Palaeozoic orogeny in Europe coincides with
the views of Zwart (1969) and Krebs & Wachendorf (1973), who emphasize the distinctive
features of the Hercynian Orogeny, especially its widespread, diffuse and protracted nature.
Zwart (1 969) suggests that 'hercynotype' orogeny occurs when continental crust drifts over
mantle with anomalously high heat flow.
3.5.3 Rotation of Europe during the Hercynian Orogeny
Because the poles defining the distinct middle to late and late Carboniferous groupings are
derived from regions throughout Europe, it is considered that Europe rotated clockwise
(about 15") as an integral block. It is unnecessary, therefore, to invoke differential local
rotations within Europe during the late Carboniferous to early Permian to explain the
declination scatter of Carboniferous NFW (e.g. Birkenmajer et al. 1968), since such scatter
in the Armorican Massif (Duff 1979a) and Bohemian Massif NRM may be explained by the
same, coherent rotation of all Europe.
This rotation and the climactic Westphalian fold deformation may have been both related
to oblique movement of the African part of Gondwanaland toward Europe; the resulting
right-lateral shear may have had a 'roller ball' effect on Europe which responded by clock-
wise rotation. This transcurrent relative movement and clockwise rotation is consistent with
structural evidence of relative right-lateral displacement between Europe and Africa during
the late Carboniferous on a megashear zone some 10 OOOkm long and lOOOkm wide
(Arthaud & Matte 1977). Palaeomagnetic observations also imply right-lateral shear dis-
placement of some 3000km between Europe and Africa during middle Triassic to Jurassic
(Irving 1977).
